section_summary: This section begins with dozens of signature sheets from a San Diego–organized petition opposing the export of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan. It then contains public and church protests, congressional referrals, and State Department replies explaining that the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation of war and did not authorize restrictions on scrap iron, gasoline, trucks, or similar commodities. A major exception is a telegram from Nanking describing Japanese control of local commerce and extensive use of American-made vehicles, aircraft, gasoline, and fuel by Japanese forces.

subfiles.title: Petition against shipments of scrap iron and war materials to Japan—signature sheets
subfiles.from: Individual petitioners assembled by the Peace Committee, San Diego
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The signers protest shipments of scrap iron and other war materials from the United States to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These pages continue a large set of identically printed petition forms bearing handwritten names and addresses, chiefly from San Diego County and other parts of Southern California. The repeated petition asks the President and Secretary of State to stop exports of scrap iron and other war material to Japan. Later correspondence identifies this installment as containing 1,076 signatures transmitted by Kate H. Dewing.

subfiles.title: Reply acknowledging Kate H. Dewing's additional petition signatures
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges 1,076 additional signatures and explains the lack of statutory authority to prohibit scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Dewing for forwarding additional signatures opposing exports to Japan. He repeats the position earlier given to W. J. Sherman: neither the President nor the Secretary of State had statutory authority to prohibit scrap-iron exports to Japan or another foreign country.

subfiles.title: Sam Weinblatt inquiry concerning American munitions supplied to Japan
subfiles.about: Weinblatt condemns the reported killing of an American child in China and asks about American munitions exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Weinblatt expresses indignation at the killing of an American child by a Japanese bombing aircraft. He asks how extensively American manufacturers are supplying Japan and what action will be taken to retard munitions exports.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Sam Weinblatt
subfiles.about: The Department describes its condemnation of civilian bombing and supplies arms-control information.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the government has repeatedly condemned the bombing of civilians and its material encouragement. He says American aircraft and aeronautical-equipment manufacturers have substantially complied with the Department's July 1, 1938 representations. The reply encloses export-license releases, the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms, and the Neutrality Act.

subfiles.title: W. R. Courtenay letter forwarding church protests
subfiles.from: W. R. Courtenay, First Presbyterian Church of Neenah
subfiles.about: Courtenay forwards protests demanding an end to American material support for Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Courtenay says members of the Neenah church support efforts to end America's partnership in Japan's war against China. He forwards a sample protest and reports that additional signed protests are being sent separately.

subfiles.title: Printed petition against American material support for Japan
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: The form petitions for practical measures to end American trade supporting Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites Japan's invasion of China, violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, and attacks on civilians and foreign institutions. It condemns American exports of aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and other materials. Despite the fall of Hankow and Canton, it calls for direct or indirect measures ending American participation in China's destruction.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. R. Courtenay
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges 305 signed protests and explains the Neutrality Act and arms-export policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Courtenay for 305 signed protest forms. He explains that a presidential finding of war would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while no statute authorized restrictions on other commodities. He cites licenses since July 1, 1937 worth about $14.27 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan, and reiterates the government's opposition to civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: George D. Hubbard letter urging an end to material aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Hubbard asks the government to stop exports of trucks, planes, gasoline, and scrap iron that aid Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Hubbard expresses alarm at the volume of American manufacturing and raw materials sent to Japan. He argues that stopping this aid would help check the slaughter and invasion intended to reduce China to economic subordination.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George D. Hubbard
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act does not permit an embargo on trucks, gasoline, or scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a war proclamation would bar arms exports to both belligerents, not Japan alone. He distinguishes statutory arms and implements of war from gasoline, scrap iron, trucks, and similar commodities, for which no embargo authority existed. The letter also provides comparative arms-export license values for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: J. Bayard Clark request for information about Japan embargo policy
subfiles.about: Clark forwards a constituent petition and requests facts with which to explain the absence of a scrap-iron embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Clark reports receiving many petitions expressing conflicting views on foreign relations. Although supportive of Hull, he says he is puzzled by the failure to embargo scrap iron and other materials to Japan. He asks for data that will allow him to explain and defend the policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. Bayard Clark
subfiles.about: Welles supplies a detailed explanation of the government's legal and policy position on exports to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to China as well as Japan. It states that scrap iron was not among the enumerated arms and that no statute authorized the President or Secretary to prohibit its export. Welles supplies arms-license totals and returns Clark's enclosed petition.

subfiles.title: Trade Agreements Division memorandum on reply to Harold Allen
subfiles.to: Office preparing the Department's reply to Harold Allen
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes language acknowledging Allen's support for reciprocal trade agreements.
subfiles.summary: The division recommends adding a paragraph praising Allen's support for restoring and expanding foreign trade through reciprocal agreements. The proposed language particularly notes the program's contribution to agriculture and general economic welfare.

subfiles.title: Harold Allen letter concerning Far Eastern policy and trade
subfiles.about: Allen raises questions about American policy toward Japan while referring favorably to the trade-agreements program.
subfiles.summary: Although the OCR is severely degraded, the letter concerns the Far Eastern situation, American exports, and policy options toward Japan. It also expresses views on reciprocal trade agreements, prompting the Trade Agreements Division's suggested acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Harold Allen
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains Neutrality Act constraints and acknowledges Allen's support for reciprocal trade agreements.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential war proclamation would stop arms exports to both China and Japan, while gasoline and other non-enumerated commodities could not be prohibited under existing law. He supplies comparative arms-license figures and refers Allen to the Commerce Department for actual export statistics. The closing paragraph welcomes Allen's support for the reciprocal trade-agreements program.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Bulkley referral of Cora Owen's Neutrality Act appeal
subfiles.about: Bulkley forwards a Women's Christian Temperance Union appeal to invoke the Neutrality Act against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Bulkley transmits a letter from Cora Owen of Fredericktown, Ohio. He summarizes her request as an appeal to invoke the Neutrality Act against Japan.

subfiles.title: Cora Owen letter on behalf of the Fredericktown WCTU
subfiles.about: Owen speaks for 38 WCTU members urging that the Neutrality Law be invoked against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Owen describes the WCTU members as peace-loving women. She asks Bulkley to work for application of the Neutrality Law so that no more war material will be sold to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Bulkley
subfiles.about: Welles suggests an explanation of the Neutrality Act for transmission to Cora Owen.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the Joint Resolution and International Traffic in Arms and offers language Bulkley may send to Owen. The explanation stresses that a war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that the act did not cover other commodities. Owen's letter is returned with the reply.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Nanking telegram 186
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a Nanking telegram concerning American contributions to Japanese military equipment.
subfiles.summary: The note points from file 894.24/489 to telegram 186 in the China file. It describes the telegram as reporting evidence of American manufacturers and supplies in Japanese equipment at Nanking.

subfiles.title: Telegram 186 from Nanking on commerce and American equipment used by Japan
subfiles.about: Smyth reports Japanese domination of Nanking commerce and extensive Japanese military use of American vehicles, aircraft, gasoline, and fuel.
subfiles.summary: The telegram describes growing Japanese commercial traffic from Shanghai, a doubling of Japanese civilians in Nanking, and Japanese control over foreign distribution and marketing. It reports that American and other foreign firms were increasingly forced to operate through Japanese agents while Japanese goods displaced foreign products. Smyth estimates that 70–80 percent of visible Japanese Army vehicles and tractors bore American manufacturers' names, notes Douglas aircraft in Japanese service, and reports American-origin gasoline and naval fuel. He contrasts these contributions with continuing Japanese interference with American rights and interests in occupied China.

subfiles.title: Schuyler C. Woodhull letter opposing exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Woodhull asks the Secretary to act against American exports assisting Japan.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten letter is largely illegible in OCR, but its subject is identified by the Department's reply. Woodhull protests the export of war and other materials to Japan and urges government action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Schuyler C. Woodhull
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why existing law did not authorize a scrap-iron embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost reviews the Neutrality Act and explains that a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan alike. Scrap iron was not an enumerated implement of war, so neither the President nor the Secretary could prohibit its export under existing law. The reply also cites arms-license values for both countries.

subfiles.title: Edwin M. Schaefer referral of Greenville College resolution
subfiles.about: Schaefer forwards a resolution adopted by the Greenville College student body.
subfiles.summary: The representative submits a resolution adopted by students at Greenville College, Illinois. The resolution concerns the Far Eastern situation and American policy toward Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Edwin M. Schaefer
subfiles.about: The Department notes that it already received the Greenville College resolution from student president John H. Schlosser.
subfiles.summary: Welles explains that John H. Schlosser had already sent the same November 4 resolution to the Department. He encloses a copy of the reply being sent to Schlosser and returns Schaefer's copy of the resolution.

subfiles.title: Kate H. Dewing letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Dewing asks Roosevelt to help stop scrap-iron exports to Japan and notes that signatures and supporting material were also sent to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Dewing says she supports Roosevelt's domestic efforts to improve living standards and economic security. She nevertheless argues that sending scrap iron to Japan is wrong and asks for help finding a less destructive basis for American trade. She writes for the San Diego Peace Committee and the local Women's International League for Peace and Freedom.

subfiles.title: Kate H. Dewing letter transmitting 1,076 signatures
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Dewing challenges the Department's export comparisons and urges an embargo on scrap iron and other essential war materials.
subfiles.summary: Dewing argues that arms-license totals understate American aid because they omit scrap iron and other essential materials, claiming that the United States supplied a dominant share of Japan's relevant imports. She presents moral, strategic, treaty, refugee, and democratic grounds for an embargo and rejects the idea that such action must be an unfriendly step leading to war. Quoting Nathaniel Peffer, she describes America as the provisioner of the Japanese Army and encloses 1,076 signatures plus a ministerial association resolution.

subfiles.title: Roy M. Pearson letter forwarding a congregational resolution
subfiles.about: Pearson forwards a church resolution opposing American participation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Pearson reports that his congregation passed the enclosed resolution the previous Sunday. He says his people feel strongly about American participation in Japanese aggression and would appreciate a reply.

subfiles.title: Swanzey Congregational Church embargo resolution
subfiles.about: The signers demand an embargo on a broad range of munitions and raw materials exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The resolution condemns Japan's bombing of Chinese cities and describes Japanese policy as military aggression. It argues that continued American shipments make the United States share responsibility for the invasion. The signers call for an embargo covering munitions, oil, gasoline, iron, aircraft, machinery, copper, automobiles, accessories, and chemicals.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Roy M. Pearson
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the congregation's resolution and explains the Neutrality Act and civilian-bombing policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Pearson for the resolution and explains that a presidential war finding would bar arms exports to both China and Japan. He states that existing law did not authorize broader commodity controls and provides arms-license totals for each country. The reply also reiterates the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and its representations to aircraft exporters.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning East Weymouth Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to a Methodist church resolution on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges a resolution unanimously passed by the church's Quarterly Conference on October 27. He explains that application of the Neutrality Act would stop arms shipments to both China and Japan and that other commodities lay outside the act. The reply includes comparative arms-license values and encloses the Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Rhode Island Congregational-Christian Conference protest
subfiles.about: Crook reports a unanimous conference request that the United States cease furnishing war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Crook states that official and visiting delegates at a well-attended Pawtucket conference unanimously opposed further American cooperation with Japan against China. He asks the President and Secretary of State to use every legitimate avenue of power and influence to stop aid to the aggressor.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frank Crook
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the Rhode Island church resolution and restates the legal limits on export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Crook for reporting the conference resolution. He explains that a Neutrality Act proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan alike and that the act did not permit controls on commodities outside the enumerated categories. The reply supplies comparative arms-license values and encloses the Joint Resolution and International Traffic in Arms.

subfiles.title: Richard J. Welch referral of Grace United Church letter
subfiles.about: Welch refers a constituent church letter opposing war-material exports to Japan for attention and advice.
subfiles.summary: Welch forwards a letter from Lloyd L. Farley of Grace United Church of the Mission in San Francisco. His office asks the State Department to consider the appeal and provide advice concerning exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Grace United Church School appeal for an embargo on aggressors
subfiles.from: Lloyd L. Farley and Elisabeth B. Lewis
subfiles.about: The church school asks its congressman to support measures refusing war materials to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Farley and Lewis argue that American sales of oil, aircraft, and other war materials helped Japan crush the Chinese people and advance its war. They ask Welch to support measures denying such materials to aggressor nations as a contribution to world peace.
